sourceTitle: The Convenient Virtue of the Perfect Consumer
scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Original film-review and environmental reading assessment, requiring independent linguistic and pedagogical validation

questions.q: Why does the author place an overflowing bin outside the film screening?
choices: To suggest that the audience never pays attention to film.
To contrast a celebrated individual habit with the host institution's arrangements.
To prove that the teenager's flask has no environmental benefit.
To explain why the documentary was not shown at a larger venue.
questions.explanation: The opening contrasts the applauded flask user with disposable cups supplied by the venue.

questions.q: Why does the author reject a simple accusation of hypocrisy?
choices: Because the overflowing bin was merely a visual effect.
Because festivals should never be expected to offer reusable cups.
Because all environmental documentaries are necessarily inconsistent.
Because this verdict ignores logistical constraints and the way responsibility is framed.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph rejects a satisfying judgement in favour of examining systems and the film's causal story.

questions.q: What advantage does the 'perfect-consumer' narrative offer a filmmaker?
choices: It makes municipal procurement rules visually dramatic.
It removes every disagreement about responsibility.
It produces clear protagonists and satisfying endings.
It reveals how all waste-processing plants operate.
questions.explanation: Personal moral choices can be filmed as simple actions with legible emotional conclusions.

questions.q: What does the absent municipal plant reveal about the documentary's approach?
choices: The film highlights a visible household habit while omitting the system receiving its results.
The family was not actually sorting its waste.
Municipal plants were prohibited from appearing on film.
The director believed recycling was always ineffective.
questions.explanation: The film praises a visible act of sorting without following what happens to the sorted waste.

questions.q: Why does the writer also reject blaming institutions alone?
choices: It would remove the need to examine the film's narrator.
It would prove that consumers have no influence on public facilities.
It would excuse the role that personal choices and civic action can play.
It would require governments to provide free metal flasks.
questions.explanation: The writer treats purchasing, voting, protest and design as mutually connected.

questions.q: Why is the metal flask not automatically the best choice in every context?
choices: Manufacture, longevity and actual use influence its environmental value.
A metal flask always costs less than a disposable cup.
Flasks are never accepted through venue security.
The material is less important than the film's music.
questions.explanation: The text points to material, production and use over time when assessing the symbol's meaning.

questions.q: What is the risk of editing the deposit-cup trial into an easy success story?
choices: It would require viewers to count cups themselves.
It would leave out missing returns, costs and design problems.
It would make the film too short to be screened.
It would show that deposit schemes never reduce litter.
questions.explanation: The trial reduces abandoned cups but reveals losses that require additional investigation.

questions.q: Why does the writer prefer a plain clipboard shot to another coastal aerial view?
choices: It would prove that the coastline is cleaner.
It would eliminate the film's emotional content.
It could replace the need to interview organisers.
It would communicate measurable returns and losses more usefully.
questions.explanation: The clipboard provides specific information about the scheme, beyond a pleasing scenic image.

questions.q: Which goal does the writer regard as too limited for environmental cinema?
choices: Questioning which institutions influence consumer choices.
Helping audiences understand competing environmental costs.
Making spectators feel morally innocent after watching.
Recognising that a personal example may influence collective habits.
questions.explanation: The conclusion rejects temporary virtue as the ultimate purpose of documentary criticism.

questions.q: What ability should viewers ideally take away from the documentary?
choices: The ability to identify missing actors, constraints and consequences in an appealing story.
Confidence that buying the right container solves systemic waste problems.
A belief that every environmental film should avoid emotion.
The certainty that institutions alone control environmental change.
questions.explanation: The writer wants audiences to question the causal explanations and omissions of environmental narratives.
